summary: RFC 5280 requires CRL issuer certificates to include keyUsage with cRLSign set, but its validation algorithm does not explicitly check for it. This Standards Track document updates RFC 5280 to clarify that check.

plainLanguage.summary: A stamp may only be used by someone allowed to use it. This adds the missing step of checking permission.

subtitle: Requiring that CRL issuer certificates explicitly carry the cRLSign capability.

tldr.problem: RFC 5280 states that CRL issuer certificates must have the keyUsage extension with the cRLSign bit set, but the CRL validation algorithm does not explicitly check for this extension's presence. This creates a security gap.
tldr.mechanism: This update modifies the CRL validation algorithm in RFC 5280 to require checking that the CRL issuer's v3 certificate actually contains the keyUsage extension and has the cRLSign bit asserted.
tldr.outcome: This prevents a subtle attack where a CA could issue a certificate without the keyUsage extension to the same subject, and that certificate could then be used to sign CRLs without the required permission check.

facts.label: Algorithm step modified
facts.value: Step (f) of CRL validation in Section 6.3.3

today: RFC 10007 is a Proposed Standard that updates RFC 5280 to clarify the CRL validation algorithm. It is the authoritative specification for this validation requirement and has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
RFC 5280 is the standard for X.509 certificates and Certificate Revocation Lists (CRLs) used on the Internet. Section 4.2.1.3 of RFC 5280 requires that CRL issuer certificates contain the keyUsage extension with the cRLSign bit asserted. This formally delegates the right to sign CRLs to that certificate holder.

However, the CRL validation algorithm in Section 6.3 of RFC 5280 does not explicitly include a check for the presence of the keyUsage extension. It only checks the cRLSign bit if the extension happens to be present. This document updates RFC 5280 to require that check, eliminating an unintended security gap.
sections.plainLanguage: X.509 certificates and revocation lists are how the Internet checks if digital IDs are legitimate. The rule says CRL signers must have permission, but the checking step was missing.

sections.title: Background on CRL Issuance
sections.content:
In a Public Key Infrastructure (PKI), a Certificate Authority (CA) can delegate the responsibility for issuing and signing Certificate Revocation Lists to other entities. This delegation occurs through the issuance of a certificate that asserts the cRLSign bit in the keyUsage extension, which indicates that the certified key may be used to sign CRLs.

When a CA delegates CRL issuance this way, the CRL issuer publishes lists of revoked certificates. These CRLs are downloaded by applications (called relying parties) that need to check whether certificates are still valid. The relying party validates the CRL by checking that the CRL was signed by an entity that holds a proper CRL issuer certificate.

Some CRLs are indirect CRLs: they revoke certificates that were not signed by the CRL issuer's CA, but by the original CA. This design allows a single CRL issuer to manage revocations for multiple CAs.
sections.plainLanguage: A big company delegates someone to publish the list of broken ID cards, and they give that person a special ID saying they can do this job.

sections.title: The Security Vulnerability
sections.content:
The gap arises from two separate flexibility rules in RFC 5280:

  1. A certificate issuer is not required to include the keyUsage extension if the certified public key is not used for signing other certificates or CRLs.
  2. The CRL validation algorithm says "if a key usage extension is present, verify that the cRLSign bit is set," but does not require the extension to be present in the first place.

These rules combined create an attack scenario: a Certificate Authority (CA) can issue two certificates to the same subject with two different keys:

  • Certificate 1: Includes the keyUsage extension with cRLSign set, used for delegating CRL signing authority.
  • Certificate 2: Contains no keyUsage extension, used for a different purpose (e.g., S/MIME signing or document signing on a secretary's laptop).

An attacker who compromises the key from Certificate 2 can then use it to sign CRLs. Because Certificate 2 lacks the keyUsage extension, the CRL validation algorithm skips the permission check and accepts the CRL as valid, even though the key was not authorized for CRL signing.
sections.plainLanguage: A company could accidentally give someone two ID cards: one with permission to revoke certifications, one without. An attacker could steal the second one and use it to revoke certifications anyway, because the check for permission was skipped.

sections.title: The Algorithm Fix
sections.content:
This specification updates step (f) of the CRL validation algorithm in Section 6.3.3 of RFC 5280. The change applies only to version 3 (v3) X.509 certificates, which support extensions:

OLD algorithm step (f): "Obtain and validate the certification path for the issuer of the complete CRL. The trust anchor for the certification path MUST be the same as the trust anchor used to validate the target certificate. If a key usage extension is present in the CRL issuer's certificate, verify that the cRLSign bit is set."

NEW algorithm step (f): "Obtain and validate the certification path for the issuer of the complete CRL. The trust anchor for the certification path MUST be the same as the trust anchor used to validate the target certificate. If the version of the CRL issuer's certificate is version 3 (v3), then verify that the key usage extension is present and verify that the cRLSign bit is set."

The new check explicitly requires the keyUsage extension to be present in v3 certificates and mandates that the cRLSign bit be asserted. Certificates in versions 1 (v1) or 2 (v2) are exempt from this requirement because those versions do not support the extensions field.
sections.plainLanguage: Now the check says: for modern ID cards (version 3), you must have permission written on the card. If the card doesn't say you can revoke certifications, it's not allowed.

sections.title: Implementation and Compatibility
sections.content:
The updated algorithm only applies to version 3 (v3) X.509 certificates, which have an extensions field. Version 1 and 2 certificates, which predate extensions and cannot include the keyUsage extension, are exempt from this check. This maintains backward compatibility with older certificate chains that may still be in use.

When implementing the new check, applications validate the CRL by examining the CRL issuer's certificate. If the certificate is v3, the application must verify that the keyUsage extension is present and that the cRLSign bit is asserted. If either condition fails, the CRL is rejected.

The specification encourages CAs to include the keyUsage extension in all certificates used for CRL signing to ensure proper validation. This is the expected practice and aligns with RFC 5280's requirement (Section 4.2.1.3) that CRL issuer certificates contain this extension.
sections.plainLanguage: Modern ID cards (version 3) must have the permission written on them. Older cards without a permission section are still okay because they can't have extensions anyway.

sections.title: Security Implications
sections.content:
The new requirement closes a security loophole but introduces a potential interoperability concern: if a CA has issued v3 CRL issuer certificates without the keyUsage extension (in violation of RFC 5280's requirement), applications implementing the updated validation algorithm will be unable to verify CRLs signed by those certificates.

To avoid such incompatibility, RFC 5280 recommends that CAs include the keyUsage extension in certificates intended for CRL verification. Additionally, if CAs have non-compliant certificates already in the wild, the policy authority managing the Public Key Infrastructure (PKI) should consider updating subject naming requirements: by ensuring that certificates used for different purposes (e.g., CRL signing versus document signing) have unique distinguished names, subject name uniqueness acts as a secondary protection against the attack.
sections.plainLanguage: Some old ID cards without permission might stop working, so companies should issue proper ones. If they can't update the cards, they can at least make sure different cards have different names so mixing them up is harder.
